title: MegDet: A Large Mini-Batch Object Detector
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition

problem.summary: Object detectors train with tiny mini-batches (2-16 images), unlike classification where batches of thousands are routine, which makes training slow, gives BN no accurate per-batch statistics, and yields imbalanced positive/negative samples; simply scaling the batch fails because a large learning rate breaks convergence while a small one loses accuracy.
statements: Mini-batch size has not been well studied for object detection, even though it is a key training factor.
Small mini-batches make detector training notoriously lengthy (ResNet-152 on COCO takes 3 days with batch 16 on 8 GPUs).
Small mini-batches cannot re-train batch normalization, so detectors keep fixed ImageNet BN statistics that mismatch COCO.
Positive/negative sample ratios are more imbalanced within small mini-batches, which may hurt final accuracy.
The large-batch dilemma: the equivalent learning rate rule demands a large learning rate, but large learning rates in detection often fail to converge, while small ones give inferior results.

evidence.quote: However, mini-batch size, a key factor for the training of deep neural networks, has not been well studied for object detection.
In contract, the mini-batch size remains very small (e.g., 2-16) in object detection literatures.
Last but not the least, the number of positive and negative training examples within a small mini-batch are more likely imbalanced, which might hurt the final accuracy.
But a large learning rate in object detection could be very likely leading to the failure of convergence

Second, in the training of detector, we usually fix the statistics of Batch Normalization and use the pre-computed values on ImageNet dataset, since the small mini-batch size is not applicable to re-train the BN layers.

background.summary: The paper sits on top of the FPN detection framework with a ResNet-50 backbone (the paper's default detector) and on large-mini-batch SGD research from image classification (linear scaling rule, warmup, generalization-gap work). The claimed gap is that large mini-batch training had been studied for classification but essentially not for detection.

relatedWork.name: FPN
relatedWork.relation: chosen as the default detection framework for its accuracy/implementation trade-off
relatedWork.quote: As FPN provides a good trade-off between accuracy and implementation, we use it as the default detection framework.

relatedWork.name: Mask R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: state-of-the-art two-stage detector with ROIAlign, one of the large-accuracy references
relatedWork.quote: Mask R-CNN [14] introduces the ROIAlign and achieves state-of-the-art results for both object detection and instance segmentation.

relatedWork.name: Goyal et al. (1-hour ImageNet)
relatedWork.relation: prior large-batch classification training with warmup that MegDet borrows its warmup policy from
relatedWork.quote: In [13], imagenet training based on ResNet50 can be finished in one hour.

relatedWork.name: Batch Normalization
relatedWork.relation: the technique MegDet is the first to re-train inside an object detection framework
relatedWork.quote: Batch Normalization [20] is an important technique for training a very deep convolutional neural network.

evidence.quote: However, the topic of large mini-batch training for object detection is rarely discussed so far.
A recent trend on CNN-based image classification uses very large min-batch size to significantly speed up the training.

solution.summary: MegDet trains a detector with mini-batches up to 256 on up to 128 GPUs by (a) re-deriving the linear scaling rule from a variance-equivalence assumption and applying a linear warmup schedule, and (b) introducing Cross-GPU Batch Normalization, which aggregates BN mean/variance across GPUs with an AllReduce so BN statistics come from enough images.
solution.approach: Scale the learning rate linearly with a gradual warmup and compute batch-normalization statistics across all GPUs instead of per device, making large-mini-batch detector training converge quickly and accurately.
components: linear scaling rule re-derived under a variance equivalence assumption
linear gradual warmup of the learning rate at the start of training
Cross-GPU Batch Normalization (CGBN) computing aggregated mean/variance via AllReduce with NCCL
sub-linear memory to fit larger BN batches (32/64 images) into GPU memory
FPN detection framework on a ResNet-50 backbone
normal and long learning-rate decay policies (epoch-based halvings)

evidence.quote: we propose a Large Mini-Batch Object Detector (MegDet) to enable the training with a large minibatch size up to 256, so that we can effectively utilize at most 128 GPUs
we present a new explanation of linear scaling rule and borrow the “warmup” learning rate policy [13] to gradually increase the learning rate at the very early stage.
we introduce Cross-GPU Batch Normalization (CGBN) for better BN statistics.
In this work, we make an attempt to perform batch normalization for object detection.

experiments.summary: All studies use COCO with a ResNet-50 + FPN detector, sweeping mini-batch size (2-256), BN batch size (2-64 images), GPU count (2-128), warmup/CGBN on or off, and normal vs. long decay policies, reporting mmAP on the 5k validation set together with wall-clock training time; the enhanced system is then submitted to COCO 2017.

benchmarks.split: hours, batch 256 on 128 GPUs vs 33.2h baseline

evidence.quote: Our MegDet (ResNet-50 as backbone) can finish COCO training in 4 hours on 128 GPUs, reaching even higher accuracy.
the 256 mini-batch experiment with 128 GPUs finishes the COCO training only in 4.1 hours
all trainings easily converge, no matter of the mini-batch size, when we combine the warmup strategy and CGBN.

limitations.summary: Without CGBN, large batches simply fail to converge and even warmup cannot save batch 128; BN statistics are only computed across GPUs on a single machine, an overly large BN batch hurts accuracy, and the observed epoch-wise learning dynamics differ from classification and are left unexplained.
items: Without batch normalization, batch-64 and batch-128 trainings fail to converge even with warmup; batch-128 fails with both warmup and half learning rate.
Larger BN statistics batches hurt: raising BN size from 32 to 64 drops accuracy, showing a mismatch between classification and detection.
Cross-GPU BN is restricted to GPUs on the same machine, limiting how many images enter the statistics.
Sub-linear memory used for larger BN batches slightly compromises training speed.
Large-batch epoch-by-epoch accuracy behaves differently from image classification, and the cause is not understood.

evidence.quote: For mini-batch size 128, the training failed with both warmup and half learning rate.
when we increase the size to 64, the accuracy drops.
Note that we only perform BN across GPUs on the same machine.
We leave the understanding of this phenomenon as the future work.

futureDirections.direction: Understand why large-mini-batch epoch-wise accuracy curves differ from those in image classification.
futureDirections.quote: We leave the understanding of this phenomenon as the future work.

futureDirections.direction: Extend the variance-based interpretation of the learning rate to wider applications beyond detection.
futureDirections.quote: We hope the variance analysis here can shed light on deeper understanding of learning rate in wider applications.

equations.name: linear scaling rule
equations.expr: r_hat = k * r when N_hat = k * N

equations.name: gradient variance
equations.expr: Var(grad l(x,wt)) = (1/N^2) * N * sigma_l^2 = sigma_l^2 / N

applications.detail: The paper positions CNN-based detectors as the mainstream in both academia and industry, and frames large-batch training as a way to exploit rapidly increasing industry compute.
applications.quote: CNN-based detectors have been the mainstream in current academia and industry.

deploymentClaims: COCO training in 4.1 hours on 128 GPUs (8x acceleration over the 33.2-hour batch-16 baseline).
Training time reduced from 33 hours to 4 hours while achieving better accuracy.
Won 1st place in the COCO 2017 Detection Challenge with 52.5 mmAP (ensemble of four detectors).
Enhanced MegDet reached 50.6 mmAP on COCO test-dev as a single submission entry.

evidence.quote: Technically, we suggest a warmup learning rate policy and Cross-GPU Batch Normalization, which together allow us to successfully train a large mini-batch detector in much less time (e.g., from 33 hours to 4 hours), and achieve even better accuracy.
Based on MegDet, we secured 1st place of COCO 2017 Detection Challenge.
